In the early 20th century, measurements of beta decay showed that electrons were emitted with a continuous spectrum of energies, appearing to violate the laws of conservation of energy and momentum.
Wolfgang Pauli proposed a neutral, lightweight particle—the “neutrino”—emitted alongside the electron during beta decay to carry away the missing energy and momentum.
Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines experimentally detected electron antineutrinos near a nuclear reactor via inverse beta decay.

have strongly disfavoured or ruled out the baseline “3+1” model across significant portions of its expected parameter space.
Alternative BSM solutions under active investigation include:
Incorporating two or more sterile states to account for complex interference patterns.
Models where a heavy sterile state decays in flight into lighter particles (e.g., a photon or scalar boson plus an active neutrino), producing the observed excess electromagnetic signals.
Hypothesising new, exotic fundamental forces or matter interactions that modify neutrino propagation without needing additional physical mass states.

The Baryon Asymmetry of the Universe

children.label: The Baryon Asymmetry of the Universe

children.value: According to the Big Bang model, equal amounts of matter and antimatter should have been created in the early universe. Had they behaved identically, they would have completely annihilated, leaving behind a universe made purely of photons.
To explain why our universe is made almost entirely of matter, Andrei Sakharov showed that three conditions must be met:
Mechanisms that change the net amount of matter.
Differences in physical behaviour between matter and antimatter.
Processes occurring during rapid cosmic expansion.
While CP violation is observed in the quark sector, it is mathematically far too small to explain the observed surplus of matter.
Leptogenesis is a primary BSM candidate for solving this puzzle using neutrino CP violation:
